card.title: Solid State: Types of Solids, Amorphous and Crystalline Solids

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: A solid is a society of fixed addresses. **Crystalline** solids repeat their addresses across the whole crystal — long-range order, sharp melting points, anisotropic properties, flat cleavage; **amorphous** solids know only their street — short-range order, a softening range instead of a melt, isotropy, irregular fracture, and the nickname "supercooled liquid" (glass, plastic, rubber).…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - NaCl mp 801 °C; MgO 2852 °C; Cu 1083 °C; diamond ~3550 °C; I₂ 114 °C - Diamond: sp³, 3-D network, insulator - Graphite: sp², layered, conductor + lubricant

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ Amorphous solids are true solids with a very high viscosity. ✅ They are regarded as pseudo-solids or supercooled liquids because they lack long-range order and flow over long times.  ·  ❌ All solids have sharp melting points. ✅ Amorphous solids soften over a range (glass-transition temperature); only crystalline solids melt sharply.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "Crystalline solids have a sharp melting point and anisotropic character, while amorphous solids soften over a range of temperature and are isotropic."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Quartz vs glass*** — identical SiO₂ chemistry; one is a crystalline solid with a sharp 1610 °C melt, the other a supercooled liquid that softens gradually — architecture is destiny.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: solid state, types of solids, amorphous, crystalline solids (within States of Matter).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Order You Can Hold Solids resist: fixed shape, fixed volume, molecules locked in place. But "solid" hides two architectures — the repeating lattice of crystals and the frozen chaos of glasses — and the classification by bonding (ionic, molecular, covalent, metallic) explains why diamond scratches glass, ice floats, and copper wires bend without breaking.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 What makes a solid - Particles (atoms, ions or molecules) are packed in **fixed positions** with only vibrational motion about them; strong cohesive forces give **definite shape and volume**, negligible compressibility, and high density compared with gases.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Crystal checklist: "order, sharp melt, anisotropy, cleavage". Amorphous = "supercooled liquid". mp ladder: diamond > MgO > Cu > I₂. Graphite = the conducting exception.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: The bonding-type table is predictive: read the bonding, predict hardness, melting point, conduction and brittleness — four properties from one classification.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Solids: fixed positions, vibrational motion only; definite shape/volume. Crystalline: long-range order, sharp mp, anisotropic, cleaves (NaCl, quartz, diamond). Amorphous: short-range order, softening range, isotropic, supercooled liquid (glass, plastic, rubber).…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Silicon's amorphous form (a-Si) coats cheap solar panels precisely because it can be deposited on glass without crystallising — disorder as a manufacturing feature.

Scientific Definitions | Term | Scientific meaning | Example | |---|---|---| | **Crystalline solid** | Long-range periodic order; sharp mp | NaCl, quartz | | **Amorphous solid** | Short-range order only; softening range | Glass, plastic | | **Anisotropy** | Direction-dependent properties | Quartz conductivity | | **Isotropy** | Direction-independent properties | Glass |…  ·  ## 4. Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 Why glass is called a supercooled liquid - Amorphous solids lack a lattice; on heating they soften progressively rather than melt sharply — the behaviour of an extremely viscous liquid frozen before it could order. Old cathedral windows are (marginally) thicker at the bottom for this reason.…  ·  ### Deep dive — crystalline vs amorphous at the particle level A crystalline solid is an **ordered, repeating array**: the same group of particles (the unit cell) repeats by translation in three dimensions, giving long-range order, sharp melting points, anisotropy (different properties along different directions) and clean geometric faces.…

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ Isotropy means the same as anisotropy. ✅ Isotropic = same property in all directions (amorphous); anisotropic = direction-dependent (single crystals).  ·  ❌ Graphite is a molecular solid. ✅ Graphite is a covalent network with strong covalent layers held by weak van der Waals forces — which explains its lubricity and conductivity.  ·  ❌ Metals melt at high temperature because they are covalently bonded. ✅ Metallic bonding strength varies widely; Hg melts at −39 °C while W melts at 3422 °C.

Common Confusions **"Amorphous" does not mean disordered entirely:** short-range order persists (a glass molecule's nearest neighbours are still regular) — it is the long range that fails.  ·  **Graphite is the exception that proves the network rule:** covalent solids are usually insulators, but graphite's delocalised π electrons conduct — quote it as the standard counterexample.
